subject: cakeCastle
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: castle made of cake.
Style: patisserie.
reasoning:
I'm planning a cake castle diorama as a single TypeScript module, deciding to keep it as a static model without joints since nothing needs to articulate, aiming for a substantial build with many parts and textures while staying mindful of API correctness since I can't test it live.

I'm sketching the diorama's structure: a silver cake board base with a lace doily texture, and a layered sponge-cake keep built from stacked cylinders painted with banded colors for sponge, jam, and cream to mimic frosting layers, plus separate frosting-top pieces.

For details I'm planning drip effects as small capsule shapes hanging off the frosting rim, keeping part counts modest since there's no joint hierarchy needed for a static model, and corner towers topped with ice-cream cone style roofs.

Walls could be slab cakes painted like piped sponge, with a chocolate bar gate arch and wafer detailing, dark chocolate window arches, and decorative touches like gummy flags, lollipop poles, strawberries, cherries, macarons, and piped rosettes scattered around.

Adding a blueberry jelly moat ring around the walls with a wafer bridge to the gate, rendered as a lathe shape with mottled blue paint and white swirl highlights, plus SVG textures for lace doily board patterning and waffle cone grids mapped onto the cone roof geometry.

For the cone roofs, I'm mixing approaches: some get a tan waffle-grid texture for the cone itself, while others get a painted frosted look with pink coloring, white sprinkle dots, and a scalloped drip edge transitioning into cream, using custom shader-style paint logic since textures can't blend with painted drips directly.

Now I'm thinking through windows: dark chocolate arched slits with a glowing candy-glass yellow interior, applied as decals onto the cylindrical tower surfaces rather than separate planes, so they wrap properly onto the painted parts.

For the gate, I want a chocolate-bar door textured with an arch, wafer squares, and gold icing trim, placed as a plane on the gatehouse front. For the flag, instead of a textured card I'll extrude a flat pennant outline with solid colors plus a small star shape, which is simpler and avoids double-sided texture issues.

For sprinkles I'm considering merging many small capsule geometries into one buffer using BufferGeometryUtils' mergeGeometries, applying individual transform matrices to each before merging since they all share consistent attributes. I still need to add icing lettering like "HAPPY BIRTHDAY" or a banner plaque on the gate.

For the piping details I'm thinking rosettes could be lathe-geometry swirls, piped borders could be small beaded spheres merged along the rim, and strawberries could be simple red spheres or cones with painted seed texture.

Macarons work as colored discs with cream filling and a ruffled cylinder foot. For the gummy bear gate guards I'm picturing merged spheres for body, head, ears, limbs, with black dot eyes and maybe a pretzel-stick spear, plus a cherry-with-stem topping the central spire.

For torch candles by the gate, I'll use the glow kit imported from agentic-3js-builder/kits/glow, keeping flame materials flat-colored since painted materials conflict with glow. I'm also planning swirl lollipop trees for the courtyard garden, using a spiral-patterned disc texture on sticks.

Rather than textured cylinder caps, I'll use two back-to-back circles for the lollipop discs since cylinder UVs get messy. I'm also adding small octahedra or cones as translucent rock-candy crystals along the moat edge, and chocolate drizzle drips on the walls using merged capsule geometry instead of full sweep extrusions. Now I'm starting to lay out the actual scene dimensions in meters, beginning with the board's radius and height.

Next I'm defining the doily sitting on top of the board, oriented flat-up using a circle plane, followed by a lathed moat ring with an inner and outer radius profile that curves into banked edges, painted with mottled blue and white highlights. I'm also planning a crumbled cookie-biscuit ring around the moat's outer edge before transitioning into a green marzipan ground layer.

Now I'm reworking that ground as a pistachio marzipan lawn disc sitting beneath the castle, with a crumbly tan cookie border further out, and considering whether the moat ring should sit raised on top of the lawn like a jelly band of water rather than carved into it.

I'm shaping the moat as a raised, bulging jelly profile for a playful effect, placing the castle on a shortbread plinth with scalloped edges, and connecting it to the lawn with a wafer-textured bridge. Then I'm laying out the castle itself—a square curtain wall with corner towers of differing heights to suggest front and back, built from thick wall boxes.

I'm adding a gatehouse at the front and a tiered central keep (three stacked cylinders of decreasing radius) topped with a spire cone, roughly totaling 0.9 units tall. I'm checking that the overall proportions work against the board radius—the castle footprint stays comfortably inside the plinth even with the corner towers extending outward.

I realize the plinth radius is too small to contain the corner towers, so I'm bumping it up to 0.42, adjusting the moat ring to sit just outside that at 0.42–0.52, and expanding the lawn and board radius accordingly to keep everything proportioned. Now I'm working out the bridge placement across the moat and sizing the wall segments between the gatehouse and corner towers.

Writing wall geometry and painting logic...

Designing distinct paint patterns per tier: chocolate sponge layers for tier1, pink polka-dot fondant with scalloped edge for tier2, vanilla for tier3, and spiral-striped cylindrical towers using angular coordinates for the stripe pattern.

I'm settling on a pastel patisserie palette for the towers—pink, cream, pistachio, and chocolate sponge colors—with towers alternating between strawberry-pink and pistachio variants for visual variety.

For the tower structure itself, I'm layering a cylindrical body topped with a wider piped collar (like a chocolate frosting ring), crenellations around that collar for a castle-like effect, and finally a cone roof nestled on top—mimicking how real patisserie castle cakes stack their tiers.

I'm varying tower heights between front (0.30) and back (0.36), and giving each roof cone a different flavor-inspired finish: pink frosting, blueberry frosting, and a chocolate-dipped waffle cone for variety.

Now I'm working through the gatehouse placement and dimensions, trying to reconcile the wall position with the gatehouse depth so the front face lines up correctly, and considering whether to top it with crenellations, a small pitched roof, or flanking cone turrets.

For the gatehouse front, I'm adding a flag with a heart, a gate door with texture, and a plaque above it — debating what text to put there, and settling on "Bon Appétit" with piped icing styling. I'm also planning arched window decals for the keep and towers.

For windows, I'll build a helper that places decals on walls facing outward, which works fine on flat boxes too. Then I need a crenellation helper that arranges boxes in a ring around a circle for battlements.

For merging geometry, I'm working out a `place()` utility that transforms a cloned geometry by position and rotation, then combines them with `mergeGeometries` before passing the result into `b.part`. Since these are static props without bones, I'm checking whether I need a root joint for safety, but it seems plain objects without joints should work fine for scenery.

I'm also confirming that merged geometries carry consistent position, normal, and uv attributes from the basic primitives, so flat-color painting won't be an issue, and I'm planning to color the crenellations with a simple cream or wafer tone.

For part counts, I'm aiming for a balance: individual explicit parts for loop-generated items like gummies, strawberries, and macarons, while merging repetitive tiny elements like sprinkles, beads, and crenels to stay within the guided range without treating it as a strict rule.

Now I'm starting the implementation file, setting up imports for THREE.js and the geometry merging utility.

Writing remaining imports...

I'm picking a builder config with "cake_castle" as the name and 2048 paint resolution for finer stripe detail, then planning to set up hex color constants and a small helper to convert hex strings into RGB values for the palette.

Writing the layered paint function...

Still designing cake layers...

Settling on the wall drip formula with a noise multiplier for variation, then sketching out a tower-building helper that takes position, height, radius, and a cake palette to construct cylindrical bodies with different roof styles (pink, blue, or cone).

Adding tower details...

I'm settling on a set of SVG-based textures to generate: doily, door, window, plaque, lollipop swirl, wafer, and a bunting banner of hanging triangle pennants strung between the front towers, building those frames along a sagging path.

Instead I'll simplify by draping the bunting from the front-left tower across to the front-right tower in a shallow arc above the gatehouse, checking it clears the door plaque height around y=0.29.

Fine-tuning: bunting curve ends at 0.335, dips to 0.305 at center, with pennants hanging down to 0.27, leaving the plaque top at 0.26 clear and gatehouse top at 0.37 safely above everything. Now I'm thinking through pennant orientation — making sure the hanging cards face forward toward the viewer by setting the flow direction so the drawn side points toward +z, the viewer's side.

Working through the geometry: since the attachment edge is the drawing's bottom, I need to draw the pennant triangle with its apex at the top and wide base at the bottom so it hangs correctly with the base near the string and the point dangling down.

Now I'm planning the overall build order to keep the implementation manageable: starting with palette constants and helper functions for placement, painting, and texture generation, then layering base elements (board, doily, lawn, moat, plinth, bridge), followed by walls, towers, gatehouse, and keep, and finally all the decorative sweets like strawberries, macarons, candles, and bunting.

Setting up the builder, seeded random function, and matrix-based placement helper, plus a merge utility to combine geometries into painted parts...

Working out the layered band pattern for the dessert texture, assigning sponge, jam, and cream regions across the vertical cycle so the proportions look right.

Now I'm writing the function for painting cone shapes, computing edges with a zigzag offset based on angle and handling the frosting mix at the boundary.

I'm defining the waffle lattice pattern on the cone surface using arc-length coordinates and a fractional diagonal check to decide dark versus golden coloring, plus the zigzag helper function.

Now I'm designing a gummy bear helper that builds the body from scaled spheres for the torso, head, ears, snout, legs, arms, and eyes, all positioned with small offsets and rotated by a given angle.

I'm applying a slight glow to make the gummy parts look translucent and glossy, then adding a thin cylinder as a pretzel spear it can hold. Next I'm starting a strawberry helper using a cell-noise paint function to create the seed pattern on the surface.

Building the strawberry body from a squashed sphere with cone-shaped leaves on top, then moving on to construct macaron shells from stacked flat cylinders.

For decoration, I'm placing a ring of macarons standing on edge along the ledge between tier1 and tier2, working out how to rotate each one so its flat face points outward tangentially rather than upward.

For the mesh colors, I'm grouping macaron shells and fillings by pastel color so I can merge geometries efficiently by batching them into color-keyed arrays before combining at the end.

Adding helper functions for beads, sprinkles, and cream swirls, using small spheres and lathe profiles to create rosette details while keeping everything in the merge buckets.

For crenellations I'm placing small alternating-colored boxes along the top edges of the walls, working out spacing and depth so they sit correctly on the wall thickness.

I'm figuring out wall positions and lengths relative to the towers and gatehouse, spacing crenel boxes along each wall while skipping the area near the gate, and considering whether to add a chocolate plinth or wafer trim along the wall base for contrast.

Now I'm placing small arrow-slit windows on the front and side walls, calculating exact x/z coordinates so they sit between the gatehouse and towers at the correct wall surface depth.

For decals, I'm working out the call parameters—target, texture, position, direction, size, and glow strength around 0.9—making sure each decal projects onto the correct wall face direction.

Then I'm double-checking the first tier's center position, radius, and height against the wall layout to confirm it fits properly behind the front wall without clipping.

Now I'm planning tiers two and three: tier2 at radius .105 with pink vanilla sponge and jam layers, tier3 at radius .07 with pistachio sponge, stacking their heights to tops of .49 and .62 respectively. I'm continuing into the roof structure—a collar disc, a frosted cone, a gold finial sphere, a cherry on top with a curved stem, and a small gold flag pole with pennant—working out each piece's radius, height, and vertical position to build up the final topper.

Thinking through tier layout now: tier2 gets a strawberry ring with sugar pearls at its ledge, tier3's ledge gets replaced by a beaded border under the overhanging roof collar since there's no room for a ledge there.
